\[

\[
 P_X\{0<|\tau_b(X)|\le t\}=\frac tc,

\]

\[

\[

where \(A_j\ge0\), \(A_j\) is supported in a region of volume \(O(h^d)\), and

\[

\]
Take a smooth squared partition of unity \(\{\chi_l\}\) at scale \(w\) on the support of \(A_j\phi_j^2\): it can be obtained by normalizing the integer translates of a fixed compactly supported bump. \[

\]
terms meet the coarse cell.

\[

{"id":"lem:uniform-bounded-overlap-fuzzy-testing","kind":"lemma","statement":"Let \(X\) be uniform on \([-1,1]^d\). Let \(0<w\le h\le1\), let \(K\le C_0h^dw^{-d}\), and let a family of fine supports have Lebesgue measure at most \(C_0w^d\) each and overlap degree at most \(D_0\). \begin{aligned}

 +(y-\tfrac12)\{v_\lambda(x)+t_0(x)u_\lambda(x)\}\\
 &\quad +(2a-1)(2y-1)
 \left\{\frac{t_0(x)}4+u_\lambda(x)v_\lambda(x)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(b_0\le a_0\), keep the same \(q_\lambda\) and instead set
\[
 p_\lambda(a,y\mid x)
 =\frac14+(a-\tfrac12)u_\lambda(x)
 +(y-\tfrac12)t_1(x)u_\lambda(x)
 +(2a-1)(2y-1)\frac{t_1(x)}4.
\]
All probabilities below are joint with the common density \(2^{-d}\) of \(X\). Direct Rademacher averaging and
\(
 t_1-t_0=4\mathbb E_\lambda(u_\lambda v_\lambda)
\)
give the exact equality of the one-observation mixtures
\[

 =\mathbb E_\lambda q_\lambda(a,y\mid x).
\]
Let \(\bar R\) be this common one-observation law. Positivity gives \(\bar p\ge\varepsilon\). Define centered likelihood perturbations
\[
 s_\lambda=\frac{p_\lambda-\bar p}{\bar p},
 \qquad
 r_\lambda=\frac{q_\lambda-\bar p}{\bar p}.
\]
They have mean zero in \(\lambda\) pointwise. Since \(u_\lambda\) and \(v_\lambda\) are linear Rademacher chaoses and \(u_\lambda v_\lambda-\mathbb E(u_\lambda v_\lambda)\) is a centered quadratic chaos, both \(s_\lambda(z)\) and \(r_\lambda(z)\) have finite Walsh expansions of degrees one and two.

We first record the coefficient comparison furnished by the displayed four-cell algebra. If \(a_0\le b_0\), the degree-one coefficients generated by \(v_\lambda\) are common to the two likelihoods and have magnitude at most \(Cb_0\). Every remaining degree-one coefficient has magnitude at most \(Ca_0\), and every remaining degree-two coefficient has magnitude at most \(Ca_0b_0\). If \(b_0\le a_0\), the common degree-one coefficients are those generated by \(u_\lambda\), with magnitude at most \(Ca_0\), while the residual degree-one and degree-two bounds are \(Cb_0\) and \(Ca_0b_0\). These assertions follow by subtracting the two displayed probabilities: their constant Walsh coefficients agree by the identity defining \(t_1-t_0\); the only quadratic term is the centered part of \(u_\lambda v_\lambda\). Division by \(\bar p\ge\varepsilon\) only changes the constant. Consequently, if
\[
 R=\max(a_0,b_0),
 \qquad D=\min(a_0,b_0),
\]
then common linear coefficients are bounded by \(CR\), residual linear coefficients by \(CD\), and residual quadratic coefficients by \(CDR\). At a fixed \(x\), at most a constant depending on \(D_0\) of these coefficients are nonzero.

\[

 \qquad
 L_Q(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\mathbb E_\lambda\prod_{i=1}^n\{1+r_\lambda(z_i)\}.
\]

Expand every factor into its Walsh coefficients and then expand the square using two independent copies of the sign vector. A term is indexed by a bipartite incidence graph: observation vertices on the two copies are joined to the one or two sign labels in the selected Walsh monomial. Rademacher orthogonality makes the term zero unless every sign label has even degree within each sign copy. Components containing only common coefficients cancel between \(L_P\) and \(L_Q\).

Consider a surviving connected component and root it at the first residual coefficient in the lexicographic order of observation index, sign copy, and sign label. If the root is a residual linear coefficient, parity forces the same sign label to occur at another observation vertex. The product at this rooted pair is bounded either by \(CDR\), when the second occurrence is common, or by \(CD^2\), when it is residual. If the root is quadratic, its coefficient is already bounded by \(CDR\), and parity forces its labels to reappear. \[

\]

\[

\[

{"id":"lem:bounded-overlap-fuzzy-testing","kind":"lemma","statement":"Let \(q\ge1\), let \(p_\star\) be a positive density, and let \(\{S_l\}_{l=1}^K\) be measurable supports whose probability under \(p_\star\) is at most \(C_0w^q\), with uniformly bounded overlap and an intersection graph of uniformly bounded degree. Let \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K\) be independent Rademacher signs. Suppose two positive density families have the same one-observation mixture \(p_\star\), give every \(S_l\) the same probability as \(p_\star\), and, after division by \(p_\star\), can be written as
\[
 \frac{p_\lambda}{p_\star}=1+A_\lambda,
 \qquad
 \frac{q_\lambda}{p_\star}=1+A_\lambda+B_\lambda+C_\lambda,
\]
where \(A_\lambda\) is linear in the signs with local coefficients bounded by \(R\), \(B_\lambda\) is linear with local coefficients bounded by \(D\le R\), and \(C_\lambda\) is a centered quadratic Rademacher polynomial with coefficients bounded by \(DR\), each coefficient being supported on the corresponding support or support intersection. Assume every density ratio obtained by adding an arbitrary subset of the residual terms is bounded above and below by fixed positive constants and preserves the support probabilities. If \(Nw^qR^2\le c_0\), then
\[
 \operatorname{TV}^2\!\left(\mathbb E_\lambda P_\lambda^{\otimes N},
 \mathbb E_\lambda Q_\lambda^{\otimes N}\right)
 \le C N^2K w^{2q}(D^2R^2+D^4),
\]
where \(c_0>0\) is sufficiently small and \(C<\infty\) depends only on the ratio, overlap, and support constants.","free_symbols":[],"depends_on":[],"proof_tex":"Let \(B_0\) bound the degree of the support-intersection graph. A greedy coloring partitions \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\) into \(L\le B_0+1\) color classes, and supports having the same color are disjoint. Assign every centered quadratic term in \(C_\lambda\) to one of the colors of its two sign indices. Starting from \(p_\lambda\), introduce the terms in \(B_\lambda+C_\lambda\) one color at a time; call the resulting density families \(p_\lambda^{(0)},\ldots,p_\lambda^{(L)}\), where \(p_\lambda^{(0)}=p_\lambda\) and \(p_\lambda^{(L)}=q_\lambda\).

Fix a color \(r\) and condition on every sign whose index does not have color \(r\). Each term added at this step contains exactly one sign of color \(r\): a quadratic term whose two indices had the same color vanishes because the corresponding supports are disjoint. Hence averaging over the color-\(r\) signs makes the added one-observation term zero. The two conditional one-observation mixtures at this step are therefore identical. Moreover, on a support \(S_l\) of color \(r\), the conditional density depends on no other color-\(r\) sign, because same-color supports are disjoint.

We now calculate the product-mixture distance at this one color step. Partition the sample space into the disjoint sets \(S_l\) of color \(r\), after assigning their null boundaries arbitrarily, and their complement. Conditional on the vector of occupancy counts \((N_l)\), the likelihood and the Rademacher prior factor over \(l\). For a cell containing \(m\) observations, divide both conditional likelihoods by their common one-observation mixture. Their factors have the form
\[
 1+\lambda_l a_i
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 1+\lambda_l(a_i+b_i)+c_i,
\]
where \(|a_i|\le CR\), \(|b_i|\le CD\), the centered term \(c_i\) has conditional mean zero and magnitude at most \(CDR\), and all denominators are bounded below by the assumed ratio constant. Expanding the two products and averaging over \(\lambda_l\), the terms involving zero or one observation agree exactly. Every surviving difference therefore contains a pair of distinct observations. Its leading coefficient is bounded by \(C(DR+D^2)\). Every additional pair of common coefficients contributes at most \(CR^2\). Thus, when \(mR^2\le c_1\), direct summation of the even Rademacher expansion gives
\[
 H_l^2\le C m(m-1)(D^2R^2+D^4)
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty(CmR^2)^j
 \le C m(m-1)(D^2R^2+D^4).
\]
This calculation uses the likelihood normalized within the cell. Consequently, arbitrary common likelihood factors in other cells have Hellinger affinity one and do not create a global second-moment multiplier.

The condition \(Nw^qR^2\le c_0\), with \(c_0\) small relative to the fixed support constant, controls the same geometric expansion after averaging over occupancies. Hellinger distance tensorizes conditionally over the disjoint cells, so
\[
 H^2\!\left(\mathbb E_{\lambda_r}(P_{\lambda}^{(r-1)})^{\otimes N},
 \mathbb E_{\lambda_r}(P_{\lambda}^{(r)})^{\otimes N}
 \mathrel{\big|}\lambda_{-r}\right)
 \le C(D^2R^2+D^4)\sum_{l:\,\operatorname{col}(l)=r}
 \mathbb E[N_l(N_l-1)].
\]
For multinomial occupancies, \(\mathbb E[N_l(N_l-1)]=N(N-1)p_l^2\), and \(p_l\le Cw^q\). Hence the last display is at most
\[
 C N^2K_r w^{2q}(D^2R^2+D^4),
\]
where \(K_r\) is the number of supports of color \(r\). Convexity of squared Hellinger distance permits averaging over the conditioned signs. The triangle inequality for Hellinger distance across the \(L\) color steps, followed by Cauchy--Schwarz and \(\sum_rK_r=K\), yields
\[
 H^2(\overline P_N,\overline Q_N)
 \le C N^2K w^{2q}(D^2R^2+D^4).
\]
Finally, \(\operatorname{TV}^2(P,Q)\le H^2(P,Q)\) under the convention \(H^2=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\), by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to \(|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\). Absorbing convention-dependent numerical factors into \(C\) proves the lemma.","status":"proved"}
